rv.q: But this play still feels overstuffed, especially when compared with the lean and fluid beauty of the rest of her formidable oeuvre.
But “Becky Nurse” waters down its impact by taking on so many plot points, it starts to feel like an overstuffed soap opera where there are too many stakes, none of them honed to an actual point.
Can I get an Amen! for a play that gives dignity to a central character who is single, working class and a grandmother with chronic pain?
This is Ruhl’s most serious work, and it also feels like her most urgent.
Becky Nurse of Salem is a weird and wonderful play with a whole lot of heart.
But in the end, Ruhl’s spiky heroine and her small but sweet circle of loved ones won me over in this supernaturally tinged family drama.
Director Polly Noonan, her cast and crew have created a production that offers audiences a complex but satisfying mix of comedy, tragedy and romance in two acts.

The problem is that Ruhl’s essay is more cogent than her play, and the negative impulse behind “Becky Nurse” throws the work off-balance, turning what could have been an absorbing character study into an overloaded, less-than-cohesive diatribe that ends on an implausible happy-ever-after note.

cn.t: Ruhl's ambitious feminist play linking 1692 Salem to modern times draws mixed reviews. Critics praise its humor and Linda Reiter's performance, but some find the plot overstuffed and complicated, with execution not quite matching its intriguing premise.
